questions.stem: Why do alveoli have thin, single-cell walls?

options.text: To minimise the distance gases must diffuse
options.explanation: A short path makes each exchange fast.
Surface area comes from the many rounded sacs, not the wall thinness.
Warmth plays no role in this adaptation story.
Defence is not what the thin wall is for.

questions.stem: What maintains a high oxygen concentration in the alveolar air space?

options.explanation: Area scales the exchange; only ventilation refreshes it.

options.text: Ventilation — fresh air brought in by breathing
options.explanation: Each breath replaces used air and tops up the oxygen.
Moisture helps gases dissolve; it does not refresh the air.
Wall thinness shortens the path; it does not renew the air.

questions.stem: Why is a good blood supply essential for gas exchange?

options.text: Because blood pressure flattens the walls
options.explanation: Pressure does not shape the gradient story here.

options.text: To store oxygen inside the alveoli
options.explanation: Blood carries oxygen away, not into storage.

options.text: It keeps delivering CO2-rich, oxygen-poor blood to maintain the gradients
options.explanation: Fresh arrivals keep both sides of the wall imbalanced.
Warming is not the capillaries' exchange role.

questions.stem: What role does the moisture layer play?

options.text: It traps dust before it reaches the blood
options.explanation: Dust trapping belongs to the upper airways' cilia and mucus.
Area comes from the sacs' rounded shapes.
Cooling is not the moisture layer's job.

options.text: Gases dissolve in it before diffusing across the wall
options.explanation: Dissolving is the first step of the crossing.

questions.stem: Which feature gives the alveoli their very large surface area?

options.text: The great number of rounded sacs
options.explanation: Many small spheres pack in more area than one large cavity.
Thinness is about distance, not area.
Moisture serves dissolving, not area.
Pleural membranes surround the lungs, not each alveolus.

questions.stem: Name the site where gases are exchanged between lung air and blood.
State four adaptations of the alveoli for gas exchange.
questions.modelAnswer: Large surface area, one-cell-thick walls, a moisture layer, and good ventilation with blood supply to keep the gradients steep.

questions.stem: Explain why the concentration gradient at the alveolus would flatten without ventilation.
questions.modelAnswer: Because exhaled air lingers: oxygen would be used up and carbon dioxide would accumulate in the alveolar space until it matched the blood's levels, and with no difference between the two sides diffusion would stop — ventilation prevents that by renewing the air.

questions.stem: At altitude the air holds less oxygen per breath. Use the alveolar adaptations to explain why climbers breathe faster.
questions.modelAnswer: Thinner air lowers the oxygen side of the gradient, so the alveolus must be refreshed more often to keep even that reduced gap steep; faster breathing raises the renewal rate, compensating for the poorer air with more ventilation per minute.
